candidate.answerReason: There are six circle pairs, each contributing at most two points. Four unit circles with distinct nearby collinear centers attain all twelve points without triple intersections.

methods.label: Bound the count and attain it
methods.explanation:
Two distinct circles have at most two intersection points. There are \(3+2+1=6\) unordered pairs among four circles: pair the first circle with the other three, the second with the two remaining circles, and the third with the fourth. Every intersection belongs to at least one such pair, so there can be at most
\[
6\cdot2=12
\]
distinct intersection points.

To show that \(12\) is possible, draw four circles of radius \(1\) with centers on one line at positions \(0,\frac12,1,\frac32\). Every pair of centers has distance greater than \(0\) and less than \(2\), the sum of the radii. Hence every pair of circles intersects at two points.

No point can lie on three of these circles. Such a point would be equidistant from three distinct collinear centers, so it would lie on the perpendicular bisectors of two adjacent segments between those centers. Those bisectors are distinct parallel lines and have no common point.

Therefore intersections belonging to different circle pairs cannot coincide. All six pairs contribute two distinct points, attaining \(\boxed{12}\). The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: The proof uses elementary pair counting, circle intersection conditions, and perpendicular bisectors. No combination formula or advanced geometry is needed.
